extracted.intended_audience: U.S. patent examiners and patent practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for conducting and supporting obviousness rejections under 35 U.S.C. 103 (MPEP § 2143–2144), including required findings, use of common sense, teaching/suggestion/motivation, reasonable expectation of success, and how to treat claim limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Known work in one field may prompt predictable variations
rubrics_metrics.description: To reject a claim based on known work being adapted from the same or a different field, Office personnel must resolve the Graham factual inquiries and articulate findings (1)–(5).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Office personnel must articulate: (1) that the scope and content of the prior art included a similar or analogous device/method/product; (2) that design incentives or market forces would have prompted adaptation of the known device; (3) that the differences between the claimed invention and the prior art were encompassed in known variations or a principle known in the prior art; (4) that one of ordinary skill, in view of identified design incentives/market forces, could have implemented the claimed variation and it would have been predictable to that person; and (5) any additional Graham findings necessary to explain obviousness. If any of these findings cannot be made, this rationale cannot support an obviousness conclusion. Examples and case law (Dann, Leapfrog, KSR, Ex parte Catan) illustrate applying this rationale, including considerations of marketplace incentives and predictable benefits of adaptation (e.g., decreased size, increased reliability, reduced cost).

rubrics_metrics.name: Some teaching, suggestion, or motivation in the prior art (T/S/M)
rubrics_metrics.description: To reject a claim on the ground that references teach or motivate modification/combination to arrive at the claimed invention, examiners must resolve the Graham inquiries and articulate specific findings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Office personnel must find: (1) some teaching, suggestion, or motivation (explicit or implicit) in the references or in knowledge generally available to one of ordinary skill to modify or combine; (2) a reasonable expectation of success; and (3) any additional Graham-based findings needed. The T/S/M test is flexible — explicit suggestion is not required; motivation may be implicit, found in the nature of the problem, or technology-independent (e.g., desire for improvements like cheaper, stronger, smaller, more efficient). Case law (DyStar, In re Kahn) supports implicit motivations and requires articulated reasoning to avoid hindsight. If any finding cannot be made, the rationale cannot be used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure of desirable alternatives does not necessarily teach away
rubrics_metrics.description: The mere disclosure of multiple alternatives in the prior art does not amount to teaching away from any of those alternatives unless the prior art criticizes, discredits, or discourages the claimed solution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An applicant's argument that the prior art 'teaches away' because it discloses a more desirable alternative is insufficient unless the prior art specifically discourages the claimed alternative. Cite In re Fulton and related case law. The Board/courts may find that the prior art as a whole still suggests desirability of the claimed combination even if not shown as the preferred alternative. See examples (shoe sole orientation, enzymatic hydrolysis reaction times).

rubrics_metrics.name: Weighing conflicting teachings of prior art references
rubrics_metrics.description: When teachings of two or more prior art references conflict, the examiner must weigh the suggestive power of each reference to determine what the combined teachings would have suggested to one of ordinary skill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider degree to which one reference discredits another and whether differences are based on comparable conditions. Examiner should analyze which reference would have more persuasive effect on the ordinary artisan. Example: In re Young (Carlisle vs. Knudsen) — later article did not sufficiently detract from the patent reference because it did not test comparable conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predictability required for combination/modification to be obvious
rubrics_metrics.description: The mere fact references can be combined or modified does not by itself establish prima facie obviousness unless the results would have been predictable to one of ordinary skill in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite KSR: if a person of ordinary skill can implement a predictable variation, §103 likely bars patentability. Examiners must assess whether the variation would have been predictable; unpredictability can defeat a prima facie case of obviousness. Consider whether techniques used to improve one device would be recognized to improve similar devices in the same way.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conclusions must be supported by articulated reasoning (no mere conclusory statements)
rubrics_metrics.description: A bare statement that a claimed invention is within the capabilities of one of ordinary skill is insufficient to establish a prima facie case of obviousness; there must be articulated reasoning with rational underpinning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners cannot rely on conclusory statements; must identify objective reasons to combine references. Cite Ex parte Levengood, KSR quoting In re Kahn. Provide factual bases and avoid hindsight reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposed modification cannot render prior art unsatisfactory for its intended purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: If the suggested modification would make the prior art device inoperable or unsatisfactory for its intended purpose, there is no motivation to modify and thus no basis for an obviousness rejection on that ground.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the modification would defeat the prior art's intended function. Example: In re Gordon — turning a gasoline strainer upside down would make it inoperable; court reversed. However, courts have sometimes found simplicity or different advantages do not necessarily teach away (In re Dance, Allied Erecting v. Genesis). Consider factual evidence and whether references reasonably suggest the modification without making the reference inoperable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposed modification cannot change the principle of operation
rubrics_metrics.description: If the proposed combination or modification would change the basic principle under which the primary reference was designed to operate, the references do not supply sufficient teachings to render the claims prima facie obvious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine whether combining references requires substantial reconstruction/re-design or a change in the fundamental principle (In re Ratti). If the claim's principle of operation is different, a prima facie obviousness rejection is improper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable expectation of success is required
rubrics_metrics.description: Where there is motivation to modify or combine the prior art, there must also be a reasonable expectation of success that the modification/combination would achieve the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite Merck, KSR, Sakraida, Anderson’s-Black Rock, Great Atlantic & Pacific Tea. Examiners must evaluate whether the prior art provides a sufficient basis for a reasonable expectation that the modification would succeed. Examples (Merck sustained rejection where prior art suggested clinical testing; Ex parte Blanc where prior art taught the antioxidant was efficient).

rubrics_metrics.name: Some degree of predictability is required; applicants may rebut with evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Obviousness does not require absolute predictability, but at least some predictability is necessary; applicants can present evidence showing there was no reasonable expectation of success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider evidence of unpredictability (e.g., scale-up failures, inconsistent experimental results). Cases (In re Rinehart, Amgen v. Chugai, In re O'Farrell) show testimony or experimental data can overcome a prima facie case of obviousness by demonstrating lack of reasonable expectation of success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predictability is determined at the time the invention was made
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether an art was predictable or whether there was a reasonable expectation of success is evaluated as of the date the invention was made (or effective filing date for AIA/FITF applications).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use contemporaneous knowledge and conditions to assess predictability. Example: Ex parte Erlich — assess motivation and expected success 'at the time this invention was made.' Editor note: for AIA/FITF matters, use effective filing date instead of time invention was made.

rubrics_metrics.name: All claim limitations must be considered in obviousness analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: All words in a claim must be considered when judging patentability over the prior art; the subject matter to be examined is defined by the terms limiting claim scope under their broadest reasonable interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners must consider grammar and ordinary meaning as understood by one of ordinary skill. Language that makes a feature optional may not limit scope. When a claim requires selecting an element from alternatives, the prior art teaches the element if one alternative is taught by the prior art (Fresenius v. Baxter). Types of claim language that may raise questions (non-exhaustive): preamble, clauses like 'adapted to', 'wherein', 'whereby', contingent limitations, printed matter, and functional language. See MPEP §§ 2111, 2181 for more. If independent claim nonobvious, dependent claims are nonobvious (In re Fine).

rubrics_metrics.name: Indefinite claim limitations must be considered
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim limitation considered indefinite cannot be disregarded; if a claim has more than one interpretation and at least one renders the claim unpatentable over the prior art, reject the claim as indefinite under 35 U.S.C. 112(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If multiple reasonable interpretations exist and one makes the claim unpatentable, the examiner should reject for indefiniteness and should also reject over the prior art based on the interpretation that renders it unpatentable. Cite Ex parte Ionescu; compare In re Wilson and In re Steele regarding reliance on speculative assumptions about claim meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations lacking support in the original specification must be considered
rubrics_metrics.description: Limitations in a claim that do not find support in the original specification (new matter) still must be considered in obviousness determinations and given weight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not ignore negative or other limitations absent from the original specification when assessing obviousness (Ex parte Grasselli). Even if a limitation was not in the original disclosure, it limits claim scope and must be considered. Failure to consider such limitations in an obviousness rejection is error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of 'common sense' in obviousness analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Common sense may inform an obviousness analysis if explained with sufficient reasoning and supported by a factual foundation; it is not a free-standing license to assert obviousness without record support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common sense has long been recognized to inform obviousness when adequately explained (Perfect Web). Examiners/courts must provide a reasoned explanation that avoids conclusory generalizations and, where basic knowledge/common sense is not based on record evidence, provide a factual foundation (In re Zurko). Identification of a specific hint or suggestion in a particular reference is not always necessary, but use of common sense must be supported by evidence or reasoning (DyStar, In re Kahn, Arendi v. Apple).

rubrics_metrics.name: If independent claim is nonobvious, dependent claims are nonobvious
rubrics_metrics.description: A dependent claim that depends from a nonobvious independent claim is itself nonobvious under 35 U.S.C. 103.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite In re Fine. Examiners should not reject dependent claims as obvious if the independent claim was properly found nonobvious.
